history_of_present_illness: Blackwater fever is characterized by a prostrating chill of asthenic type, more severe than typical malarial chills, often following resistance-lowering influences like sun exposure, rain, dietary/alcoholic excesses, or quinine administration. The attack is sudden, with marked prostration, pain over the kidneys, and a rapid temperature increase to 104°-105°F. This is accompanied by early and intense jaundice and the passage of reddish to black, porter-colored urine (haemoglobinuria). Nausea, bilious vomiting, and epigastric distress are common. The fever course may be intermittent, remittent, or continuous, often followed by profuse sweating and marked debility. The pulse is initially rapid (110-120 bpm) but becomes feeble and of low tension, potentially thready and very rapid (150+ bpm) in severe cases, with pallor and cold extremities. Other symptoms include epistaxis, hiccough (an unfavorable sign), rapidly developing severe anemia (loss of 2 million red cells in 24 hours), and in severe cases, anuria leading to uraemic symptoms like coma and convulsions. Patients typically remain mentally clear but experience restlessness and marked anxiety.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Blackwater fever primarily affects old European residents in tropical regions where malignant tertian malaria is prevalent and intense, particularly those who have suffered repeated malarial attacks. It is rarely associated with benign tertian or quartan infections. The disease is endemic in tropical Africa (West, Central, East, 12° N to 12° S latitude), Southern Italy, Sicily, Sardinia, Greece, Central America, Northern South America (Amazon basin), and malarious sections of the Southern U.S. (Arkansas, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, South Carolina), though it is becoming rarer there. It was noted among British forces in Macedonia and Palestine during WWI. While almost eradicated among Americans in the Panama Canal Zone due to malaria prophylaxis, it remains common among white Europeans who neglect it. Malaria is considered the predisposing cause. Exciting factors include another malarial attack, administration of acid salts of quinine (especially in large doses), refrigeration (e.g., wet clothes followed by chilling sea breeze), excessive fatigue, or dietetic/alcoholic excesses. Quinine administration, particularly with refrigeration, is the most common exciting factor. The disease is linked to red cell haemolysis, possibly due to autolysins or anaphylactic sensitizations from previous malarial damage. It is believed that proper and persistent malarial prophylaxis (quinine or other antimalarial measures) keeps blackwater fever in check or prevents it. Susceptibility is higher in those careless about quinine prophylaxis or exposed to depressing influences like cold, wet, excessive fatigue, or alcoholic debauches. Overexertion and chilling are common triggers. Individuals in bad health or with poor diets are more susceptible. Europeans are generally exempt during their first year in endemic areas.
vitals: Temperature rapidly increases to 104° to 105°F. Pulse is rapid, 110 to 120 bpm initially, becoming feeble and low tension; in severe cases, it can be very rapid, almost thready, at 150 bpm or more.
physical_exam: Patients present with a prostrating, asthenic chill, marked prostration, and severe pain over the kidney region. Early and intense jaundice appears within hours, lasting for several days, without skin itching. Profuse sweating accompanies fever reduction. Nausea, bilious vomiting, and epigastric distress occur early. The spleen and liver are enlarged and tender. Severe cases may show pallor, cold extremities, and a thready pulse. Epistaxis and hiccough (an unfavorable sign) may be present. Urinary findings include reddish to black, porter-colored urine (haemoglobinuria) and potentially vesical tenesmus. Rapidly developing anemia is striking. Patients often exhibit restlessness and marked anxiety while remaining mentally clear.
labs_and_diagnostics: The disease is characterized by excessive destruction of red cells, leading to haemoglobinaemia and haemoglobinuria due to the liver's inability to process liberated haemoglobin. Active haemolysins are demonstrated in tissues and urine, but without increased red cell fragility or auto-haemolysis. Pathological findings include congestion of kidneys with purple-colored pyramids, prominent Malpighian bodies in the spleen, focal necroses in the spleen and liver, and marked destruction of liver cells around central veins. The myocardium shows fatty change, and adrenal fat lipoid content is reduced. Anuria is attributed to mechanical plugging of renal tubules by haemoglobin casts. Urine is reddish to black, containing granular débris with haematoidin crystals and rarely red cells (distinguishing it from haematuria). Spectroscopically, absorption bands of methaemoglobin (and rarely oxyhaemoglobin) are noted. Large quantities of albumin and urobilin are present, with abundant casts. Blood tests show rapid and marked anemia (up to 2 million red cells destroyed in 24 hours), reduced red-cell count, and hemoglobin percentage. The blood is thin with delayed coagulation time, and smears are difficult to make. Melaniferous leucocytes may be found, and large mononuclears and transitionals may increase to 20% during post-paroxysm leucopenia. Blood alkalinity and coagulability are reduced. Serum shows haemoglobinaemia and potentially reduced alkalinity. Urine may be very acid with large amounts of acetone bodies. Diagnostic tests for blood in urine include haemin-crystals, guaiac, or benzidin tests. Evidences of malarial infection (parasites or melaniferous leucocytes, increased large mononuclear percentage) are usually present.
differential_diagnosis: Blackwater fever is clinically differentiated from: Yellow fever, which has a slower jaundice onset (after 3rd day), no blood in urine before 3rd-4th day (then haematuria), albuminuria from 2nd day, no splenic enlargement, Faget’s sign (stationary pulse with rising temperature or falling pulse with stationary temperature), and mucus-like vomiting followed by black vomit around the 4th day. Malarial evidence is negative in yellow fever. Bilious remittent malarial fever, which has a slower onset, bile in urine (yellow froth on shaking), slower jaundice development (around 2nd day), marked splenic enlargement (may have ague cake), less rapid pulse, and less severe bilious vomiting and gastric distress than blackwater fever, with malarial evidence almost always obtainable. Infectious jaundice, where jaundice appears later (48-72 hours), pulse is slow, no haemoglobinuria (though haematuria may occur), and polynuclear leucocytosis is present. Very mild cases of paroxysmal haemoglobinuria in blackwater districts are difficult to differentiate. Other causes of haemoglobinuria include chlorate of potash or carbolic-acid poisoning, snake bite, or severe burns.
management_and_clinical_course:
The mortality rate varies, with reported rates of 25.9% in quinine-treated cases and 11.1% in untreated cases. Prognosis is poor with marked and persistent vomiting, hiccough, and especially anuria, which often leads to uraemic complications and is a primary cause of concern. A severe attack results in marked anemia and protracted convalescence.

**Prophylaxis**: Proper and persistent malarial prophylaxis (e.g., quinine or other antimalarial measures) is paramount to prevent blackwater fever. For individuals with a history of blackwater fever, quinine prophylaxis should use quinine tannate or quinine base, avoiding acid salts. Patients should avoid chilling influences, conditions that lower resistance, errors in diet, alcoholic excesses, exposure to wet, and irregular quinine prophylaxis, especially after two to three years in highly malarious tropical regions.

**Treatment**: Absolute bed rest, avoidance of chilling, and good nursing are crucial. Freely administer alkaline waters (e.g., Vichy, or water with 30 grains bicarbonate of soda per pint). Cracked ice helps reduce nausea and vomiting. Albumin water or barley water may be better tolerated than milk or broths. Ensure patient nourishment, even in the initial asthenic stage. Hot fomentations to the loins relieve pain and assist renal congestion. Saline enemata are valuable for mild cases, while subcutaneous or intravenous saline injections are needed for severe cases. Sorel recommends intravenous or enema administration of lactose (92.5g/1000cc water) or glucose (47g/1000cc water) solutions (approx. 300cc). Dry cupping or hot fomentations over the loins are used for threatened anuria. Intravenous 1-2% bicarbonate of soda solution may be indicated for diminished serum alkalinity. For urinary suppression, very hot salines administered high in the colon via a double-flow tube are recommended. Regarding quinine during an acute attack, many authorities withhold it for the first one to two days; if parasites persist after two to three days, quinine is indicated, or if parasites are present on day one (by some). Quinine, if given, should not be orally. Calcium lactate (20 grains every four hours) has been suggested but lacks strong evidence. Burkitt reports excellent results with intravenous alkaline solutions and neosalvarsan. Hearsey suggests a mixture of 10 grains bicarbonate of soda and 1/30 grain bichloride of mercury every two hours. Cholesterin (15-grain doses in thick milk every four hours, 2-3 times) is given as an anti-haemolytic. Small, divided doses of calomel can be used to keep bowels open. Antipyretics are contraindicated due to their depressant effect on the heart. Blood transfusion has been practiced but reports indicate only temporary improvement followed by a return of haemoglobinuria.
